raw:
The ten hypotheses below are the conditional effects best supported by the 100 experiments. Most rest on two or three parents per condition, so they are directional bets.

1. **Edge 3 → skip_connect helps more when edge 3 was `none`.** Restoring the direct input-to-output path gave the largest gains in the data: IN16 rose 15.96, 18.67 and 18.04 points (experiments 71, 75, 78).
2. **Edge 3 → nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 3 was `none`.** All three such cases (11, 15, 18) improved on all datasets, by up to 9.95 points on IN16.
3. **Edge 3 → nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 was skip_connect.** All three such cases (12, 16, 19) got worse on every dataset.
4. **Edge 0 → none hurts more when edge 1 is `none`.** Removing both inputs to the inner nodes collapses the cell to edge 3 alone. Those cases (25–27) lost 10–20 points on IN16, versus about 0–3 points elsewhere.
5. **Edge 5 → nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 0 is `none`.** With node 1 dead, the convolution on edge 5 is the main learnable path. It gained 8.7–10.5 points on IN16 (8–10), versus mixed results otherwise.
6. **Edge 0 → nor_conv_1x1 helps more when it replaces avg_pool_3x3.** Those cases (84, 87, 90) gained the most on all three datasets.
7. **Edge 1 → nor_conv_3x3 helps more when it replaces avg_pool_3x3.** Cases 54, 57 and 60 gave the largest gains among the edge 1 edits.
8. **Edge 5 → avg_pool_3x3 is less harmful when edge 5 was `none`.** Adding a path is better than swapping out a convolution for pooling: case 70 was clearly positive, while most replacements lost points.
9. **Edge 0 → none hurts less when it removes avg_pool_3x3.** Removing a parameter-free pooling edge cost less than removing a convolution (23 and 30 versus 21 and 24).
10. **Edge 2 → none hurts less when edge 5 is `none`.** Node 2 then has no outgoing edge, so removing an edge into it matters little. This shows in the mild, mixed changes in 95–97.
